title: can and could
subtitle: I can / I could
summary: Use can and can't for now, could and couldn't for the past, and Can you ... ? / Could I ... ? to ask people for things.

lesson.heading: He can play the piano
lesson.text: A man stands at a big piano. He says: 'I can play the piano.' At an office door, a man with two heavy bags says to a woman: 'Could you open the door, please?' **can** + verb says what somebody knows how to do or what is possible.

lesson.heading: The form
lesson.note: In questions can comes first: **Can** you **swim**? **Can** he **play** chess?

lesson.heading: I can do something
lesson.text: **I can** do something = I *know how* to do it, or *it is possible* for me to do it.

examples.text: I **can play** the piano. My brother **can play** the piano too.
Sarah **can speak** Italian, but she **can't speak** Spanish.
'**Can** you **swim**?' 'Yes, but I'm not a very good swimmer.'
I'm having a party next week, but Paul and Rachel **can't come**.

lesson.heading: For the past: could / couldn't
lesson.text: For the past (yesterday, last week etc.), we use **could** and **couldn't**.

examples.text: When I was young, I **could run** very fast.
Before Maria came to Britain, she **couldn't understand** much English. Now she **can understand** everything.
I was tired last night, but I **couldn't sleep**.
I had a party last week, but Paul and Rachel **couldn't come**.

left.label: now: can / can't
examples: I'm having a party next week, but Paul and Rachel **can't come**.
Kate doesn't know what to do. She **can't decide**.

right.label: past: could / couldn't
examples: I had a party last week, but Paul and Rachel **couldn't come**.
I was tired last night, but I **couldn't sleep**.

lesson.heading: Can you ... ? Could I ... ?
lesson.text: We use **Can you ... ?** or **Could you ... ?** when we ask people to do things. We use **Can I have ... ?** or **Could I have ... ?** to ask for something, and **Can I ... ?** or **Could I ... ?** to ask if it is OK to do something.

examples.text: **Can you** open the door, please? *or* **Could you** open the door, please?
**Can you** wait a moment, please? *or* **Could you** wait ... ?
*(in a shop)* **Can I have** these postcards, please? *or* **Could I have** ... ?
Tom, **can I** borrow your umbrella? *or* Tom, **could I** borrow your umbrella?
*(on the phone)* Hello, **can I** speak to Gary, please?

lesson.text: can and could never change and never take to: she **can swim**, not ~~she cans swim~~ or ~~she can to swim~~.

exercises.prompt: You want to know if Steve is able to ski. You ask him: '___?'
exercises.explanation: In questions can comes before the subject: Can you ski?

exercises.prompt: I like this hotel room. You ___ the mountains from the window.
exercises.explanation: It is possible to see them, so: You can see the mountains.

exercises.prompt: You are speaking very quietly. I ___ you.
exercises.explanation: It isn't possible for me now: I can't hear you.

exercises.prompt: Match each situation with the right question.

pairs.left: Your arms are full and you need the door opened.
pairs.right: Could you open the door, please?

pairs.left: You are at dinner and you want the salt.
pairs.right: Could you pass the salt, please?

pairs.left: You want to borrow Tom's umbrella.
pairs.right: Tom, could I borrow your umbrella?

pairs.left: You are on the phone and you want to talk to Gary.
pairs.right: Hello, can I speak to Gary, please?

pairs.left: You are in a shop and you want some postcards.
pairs.right: Can I have these postcards, please?

exercises.prompt: You want to know if Steve is able to play chess. Ask him.
exercises.explanation: Can + you + verb, with no to.

exercises.prompt: Catherine got the job because she ___ five languages.
exercises.explanation: She knows how to speak them: she can speak five languages.

exercises.prompt: I wasn't hungry yesterday. I ___ my dinner.
exercises.explanation: Yesterday is the past, so we use couldn't.

exercises.statement: When I was young, I can run very fast.
exercises.explanation: When I was young, I could run very fast. For the past we use could.

exercises.prompt: James ___ to the concert next Saturday. He has to work.
exercises.explanation: Next Saturday is not the past, so we use can't: James can't go.

exercises.prompt: Paula ___ to the meeting last week. She was ill.
exercises.explanation: Last week is the past, so we use couldn't + verb: couldn't go.

exercises.prompt: You are in the library and you have nothing to write with. You ask the person next to you: '___ your pen, please?'
exercises.explanation: Can I ... ? or Could I ... ? asks if it is OK to do something.

exercises.prompt: Is the sentence about now or about the past?

items.text: When I was young, I could run very fast.
Sarah can speak Italian, but she can't speak Spanish.
I was tired last night, but I couldn't sleep.
Paul and Rachel can't come to my party next week.
Before Maria came to Britain, she couldn't understand much English.
Have you seen my bag? I can't find it.
